description: Yemen's healthcare system is under increasing pressure as renewed fighting across several front lines sends more wounded patients to hospitals already struggling with severe funding shortages. More than 60 wounded patients were admitted in the week following an escalation in fighting in September, many requiring emergency surgery and blood transfusions. The hospital also provides specialised treatment for patients with chronic bone infections, congenital deformities and bone cancer. Its director says the facility continues to operate on a budget unchanged since 2014, despite a dramatic decline in the Yemeni rial's value. author: Al Jazeera English
description:
It all starts with an undercover meeting about a murder for hire. An admitted member of a Northern Irish paramilitary group called the Ulster Volunteer Force, the UVF, says he can arrange to have a man killed. So, we travel to Belfast to track him down. In this episode, Al Jazeera Investigates the violent factional history of the UVF and how the organization has evolved and expanded since the 1998 Good Friday peace agreement. What happens to paramilitary group when the fighting stops? They don’t go away, they adapt and in the case of the UVF, it has become a violent, international drug cartel willing to sell its services to the highest bidder.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
From Gaza and Ukraine to Sudan, the United Nations has repeatedly faced criticism for failing to stop wars and protect civilians. But what if some of its most controversial failures are not flaws in the system, but consequences of how it was designed?

In 1945, the world’s most powerful countries struck a bargain: they would join a new international organisation, but retain the power to block major Security Council decisions.

More than 80 years later, that arrangement still shapes global diplomacy.

Al Jazeera explains how the UN veto works, why five countries hold extraordinary power over international peace and security, and why reforming the Security Council remains so difficult.

The question isn’t simply why the UN fails to act. It’s whether the world can change a system built to accommodate its most powerful countries.
